paper_title: VibeGame: Prompt-to-Game Development with AI-Native Engine and Self-Evolving Adversarial Agent Team

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Large language model agents have enabled software development through natural-language interaction, but extending this paradigm to end-to-end game development remains challenging. Building a playable game requires coordinating code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, while allowing developers to validate their integrated behavior through interactive testing. We introduce VibeGame, a framework for creating complete 2D game projects from natural-language prompts and optional reference images. Its AI-native game engine represents project state as schema-validated structured text and provides frame-synchronous runtime control, enabling agents to inspect game states, execute actions, and verify behavior at their own pace. Built upon this interface, we design an Adversarial Agent Team of eight specialized agents to separate implementation from review, so that problems are found and fixed through multi-round loops. For each conducted and accepted project, we further introduce a training-free self-evolution mechanism to distill it into reusable skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts for future development. We evaluate prompt-assets-to-game (PA2G), where agents are given an asset library, and prompt-to-game (P2G), where agents generate their own art. On a GameCraft-Bench subset, VibeGame in P2G consistently outperforms a range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G with the same underlying model, including GPT-6.1-Sol.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Games are among the most demanding types of software to develop: they must sustain interactive worlds in real time, maintain coherent visual identity, and enforce consistent, balanced rules. Meeting these requirements has traditionally required months of collaboration among designers, programmers, and artists using game engines such as Unity [1], Unreal Engine [2], and Godot [3]. The required time and resources put game development out of reach for many creators. Artificial intelligence (AI) has begun to lower this barrier from two directions, yet neither fully supports practical game creation. World models such as Genie [4] generate interactive experiences directly from video but produce no editable source code, while large language models (LLMs) integrated into commercial engines, as in DreamGarden [5] for Unreal, face project state scattered across graphical interfaces and binary assets that agents cannot consistently inspect or modify. Neither produces complete game project that can be built, played, inspected, versioned, and iteratively revised. Meanwhile, LLM-based coding agents [6, 7] have made vibe coding increasingly accessible, allowing nonprogrammers to describe software in natural language and refine it through iterative feedback. Games are the natural next step, and we formulate this challenge as Prompt-to-Game (P2G) Development: given only natural language description and optional reference images, the system must produce complete playable game project, discovering and fixing its problems along the way. Recent systems and benchmarks have made progress toward this goal. AutoUE [8] and OpenGame [9] build games end to end with agents, and GameDevBench [10] and GameCraft-Bench [11] evaluate such abilities, the latter also with provided asset library, setting we call Prompt-Assets-to-Game (PA2G). However, most of these efforts reserve runtime checks for final evaluation or limit them to verifying that game builds and runs. 2 Figure 2 Games created by VibeGame from prompts across diverse 2D game genres. Yet many game issues emerge only during play, making interactive testing and refinement essential to playability. Additionally, fixing one project artifact can introduce inconsistencies across interdependent code, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations. Addressing these challenges reliably and carrying validated solutions forward to future projects requires three tightly coupled capabilities. First, an agent-operable project state must expose the structure and dependencies among scripts, scenes, assets, animations, physics, and configurations, because direct file access alone cannot prevent seemingly local edit from violating hidden relationships elsewhere. Second, interactiongrounded verification is needed because structurally valid project can still fail at runtime when player input, physics, animation, and game logic interact; since execution unfolds faster than an agent can reason about it, verification requires controllable execution that can be paused, advanced, and examined. Third, the system must preserve validated development experience: so that reusable project structures, features, and coordination procedures can guide subsequent work, while unverified or project-specific content must remain isolated. To address these requirements together, we introduce VibeGame, unified framework that connects project construction, runtime verification, and experience reuse within development loop, as illustrated in Figure 3. (1) An AI-native game engine exposes scenes, nodes, assets, scripts, and configurations as structured text with explicit references and schema validation, and its frame-synchronous runtime control lets agents inspect game states, inject actions, and observe their consequences. (2) Built upon this interface, an Adversarial Agent Team (AAT) separates implementation roles from auditor, player, and reviewer roles, which challenge the game from structural, behavioral, and project-level perspectives; the team iterates review and revision until the project satisfies the intended design and functionality. (3) Once the project is accepted, trainingfree self-evolution mechanism distills its reusable experience into project skeletons, verified modules, and collaboration contracts (Section 3.3), which subsequent projects adapt and revalidate rather than reuse blindly. Figures 1 and 2 present some examples produced by VibeGame. And with the same underlying model, VibeGame in P2G outperforms range of agent harnesses in either P2G or PA2G. Ablation studies further show that removing either the AI-native engine or the adversarial review roles substantially lowers the overall score, and that the experience distilled through self-evolution with stronger model can be transferred to improve weaker one. In summary, our contributions are three-fold: We introduce VibeGame, framework for prompt-to-game development that transforms naturallanguage prompts into complete, playable game projects, enabling rapid game creation and subsequent 3 iterative refinement. At the core of our method is an AI-native game engine that enables coding agents to directly inspect and modify project state and control runtime execution without relying on graphical editors. Building on this engine, we introduce an Adversarial Agent Team that separates implementation from review, together with training-free self-evolution mechanism that distills validated development experience into reusable knowledge for future projects. We comprehensively evaluate VibeGame against other mainstream agent harnesses in both P2G and PA2G settings, demonstrating superior performance over all of them.

sections.title: 2 Related Work
sections.content: Agentic software development and vibe coding frameworks. Coding agents such as Claude Code [6], Codex [7], Cursor [12], OpenHands [13], and SWE-agent [14], often with ReAct [15]-style reasoning and evaluated on benchmarks such as SWE-bench [16], have moved LLM-based programming to repository-level development. Vibe coding frameworks such as Trellis [17] externalize specs, tasks, and memory as persistent repository artifacts, and ChatDev [18] and MetaGPT [19] introduce role specialization into software development. VibeGame extends these directions to game projects, where code, art assets, scene configurations, and runtime behavior must be maintained jointly and verified by running the game. Engine-integrated game generation. Prior work connects LLMs and generative models to game engines and 3D tools: Sketch2Scene [20] builds 3D game scenes from sketches; UnrealLLM [21] and DreamGarden [5] generate content and environments in Unreal Engine (UE); 3Dify [22] uses the Model Context Protocol (MCP) [23] or computer use to call Blender [24], Unity, and UE toolchains, enhanced by retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) [25]; and Hassan [26] generate Unity templates from design documents. AutoUE [8] chains five agents to generate 3D games in UE and uses play-testing for the final evaluation. These systems mostly work around the graphical user interface (GUI) workflows of commercial engines, whereas web frameworks like Phaser [27] express projects fully in text. OpenGame [9] builds on Phaser with templates and debug protocol, generates its own assets from the prompt alone, i.e., the P2G setting, and repairs build and test failures until the game builds and runs. VibeGame further adds an agent-oriented project representation, runtime control, and visual verification, and lets independent roles verify the running game inside the development loop.

sections.title: 3 The VibeGame Framework
sections.content: VibeGame takes natural-language request and optional reference images as inputs and produces complete 2D game project that can be run, inspected, and modified through later requests. Figure 3 presents the project lifecycle. The AI-native engine provides the shared project representation and runtime interface on which all agents operate (Section 3.1). On top of it, the Adversarial Agent Team, eight specialized agents coordinated by an orchestrator, turns the request into an accepted game through intention alignment, parallel development, and adversarial correction (Section 3.2). After acceptance, the trainingfree self-evolution mechanism distills the project into skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts that initialize future runs (Section 3.3).

sections.title: 3.1 AI-Native Game Engine
sections.content: A game engine provides the foundation on which game project is constructed and executed, but traditional engines are designed for human-operated workflows. We define game engine as AI-native when it has three properties that remove the resulting barriers for coding agents. (1) GUI-Independent: the entire project is represented as plain-text files that agents can inspect and edit directly, rather than engine-specific identifiers or binary files that require graphical editors. (2) Runtime-Accessible: agents can pause, step through, observe, and intervene in the running game through code rather than GUI-based debugging tools, turning an asynchronous real-time system into synchronously verifiable process. (3) Source-Available: agents can inspect the engines uncompiled source code rather than relying on documentation that may lag behind version changes or omit implementation details. 4 Figure 3 System overview of VibeGame. (a) The Adversarial Agent Team turns user request into an accepted game through intention alignment, parallel development, and adversarial correction. (b) The AI-native game engine exposes structured project representation and frame-synchronous runtime control for implementation and playtesting. (c) Training-free self-evolution extracts skeletons, modules, and collaboration contracts from accepted projects and returns them to future development as project priors. GUI-Independent. We build our engine on Phaser because it expresses projects fully in text (Section 2). However, Phaser imposes little structure on how project is organized, which makes agent-generated projects prone to fragmentation. We therefore represent each game as collection of scenes whose configurations are stored in type-checked JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) files. Each scene is hierarchy of nodes, the basic building blocks of the project; node groups its visual appearance, collision geometry, behavior scripts, and configuration into one unit, declared explicitly in JSON fields rather than hidden inside constructors. Nodes shared across scenes are stored as standalone definition files and instantiated at runtime. This scene-nodeasset hierarchy gives every artifact clear location and makes cross-file dependencies explicit, so schema validation can detect invalid references, such as missing assets, before execution rather than as runtime failures. Runtime-Accessible. structurally valid project may still fail when player input, physics, animation, and game logic interact during execution. We therefore expose the running game through frame-synchronous programmatic interface: agents can pause and resume execution, advance specified number of frames, inspect or modify runtime properties such as node positions and velocities, inject semantic actions such as press jump, and capture screenshots. With these controls, agents verify runtime behavior at their own pace through frame-by-frame inspection, scripted test sequences, or heuristic bots that react during real-time play. Source-Available. Even with structured project files and runtime control, agents may still encounter engine behavior that the documentation does not fully explain, particularly after an interface change or in uncommon functionality. We therefore copy the engines complete, uncompiled source code into the project directory at initialization, so agents can look up the exact application programming interfaces (APIs), assumptions, and implementation details needed for the current task.

VibeGame therefore introduces an Adversarial Agent Team (AAT) comprising eight specialized roles: orchestrator, designer, artist, architect, programmer, auditor, player, and reviewer. We define each agents responsibilities through role-specific prompts and execution hooks, and use persistent project artifacts to preserve decisions and communicate them across the team. Throughout this process, the orchestrator maintains the development state and coordinates the specialized roles. 3.2.

sections.title: Intention Alignment
sections.content: Before development begins, the designer draws on game-design principles and genre conventions to expand requests such as make Hollow Knight-style boss fight into complete Game Design Document (GDD) that defines gameplay mechanics, progression rules, and numerical systems. In parallel, the artist uses image-generation models to create concept art that establishes consistent visual direction for subsequent assets. After user confirmation, the GDD and concept art form the shared ground truth for all downstream development and evaluation. During development, any task that introduces or changes design decision returns to the designer, who drafts it, confirms it with the user, and merges it into the GDD.

sections.title: 3.2.2 Parallel Development
sections.content: Code Workflow. Code is implemented by pipeline of four agents: architect, programmer, auditor, and player. The orchestrator first decomposes the game into parallel components, retrieves relevant skeletons, modules, and contracts from the self-evolution repository (Section 3.3) as project priors, and prepares Product Requirements Document (PRD) that defines the scope and acceptance criteria of each component. The architect then plans the implementation strategy and its verification procedure, and after the orchestrator approves the plan, the programmer implements it. The auditor checks the result statically with the engines consistency-checking tools and against the design specification. Finally, the player runs the game through the engines runtime interface under frame-synchronous control and uses vision model to assess whether the rendered result matches the intended appearance. sub-task is complete only after it passes both static 6 auditing and runtime play-testing. Artist Workflow. The artist agent converts visual requirements from the orchestrator into engine-ready assets. It invokes image-generation models, including GPT-Image-2 [31] and Nano Banana Pro [32], to create the initial artwork, then applies post-processing operations such as background removal and size normalization. It then registers the processed assets with the engine, recording their paths, dimensions, and usage.

sections.title: 3.2.3 Adversarial Correction
sections.content: After all sub-tasks are completed, an independent reviewer acts as the final quality gate and evaluates the complete project on functionality (whether the game behaves as specified), visual quality (asset completeness, stylistic consistency, and screen clarity), and playability (e.g., control responsiveness and the clarity of combat feedback). If the project fails any criterion, the reviewer rejects it with specific reasons, and the orchestrator converts them into new repair tasks; this build-review cycle continues until the project satisfies all acceptance criteria. The process runs automatically by default, and the orchestrator incorporates any user feedback into subsequent development.

sections.title: 3.3 Training-free Self-Evolution
sections.content: The AI-native game engine and AAT produce accepted game projects that reflect both agent-side implementation and user feedback. VibeGame distills reusable experience from these validated projects with training-free self-evolution mechanism and uses it to initialize future development runs, preserving implicit development knowledge that general-purpose agents lose across independent runs. We organize the experience into three complementary forms: skeletons, modules, and contracts. Skeletons. skeleton is runnable project template associated with particular game type. It removes project-specific art assets but preserves the code architecture, tuning values, visual proportions, scene flow, and runtime structure of the original project. Each skeleton also includes error notes and an art pack. The error notes summarize recurring failures and their verified fixes, while the art pack records reusable visualproduction recipes, including asset-generation prompts and post-processing conventions for the corresponding game type. Modules. module is self-contained behavior script that can be attached to any node (Section 3.1) and implements functionality reusable across game types. In addition to the underlying behavior, module may include self-checking logic that converts previously observed runtime failures into static validation rules executed before the game starts. Contracts. contract is document that adapts the general AAT workflow to recurring feature or development pattern. It specifies the role-specific inputs, outputs, dependencies, and verification criteria required to implement that feature, enabling agents to coordinate through validated procedure rather than relying only on the generic build-and-review loop. For example, map contract defines how the designer specifies map requirements, how the programmer represents the map in project files, how the artist supplies the required assets, and how the auditor and player verify the completed result.

Benchmark. We randomly sample two tasks from each of the 15 game types in GameCraft-Bench [11], 30

input setting, and a short hint on demo recording, leaving the game descriptions and evaluation rubrics

and P2G settings, giving every harness, including VibeGame, a 24-hour budget per task with its model at
the xhigh reasoning effort; in P2G, harnesses without native image generation are given the same image
generation model as VibeGame. Because GPT-5.5 [33], the judge used by GameCraft-Bench, makes various
judgment errors, we use GPT-6.1-Sol [34] as the judge instead. Appendix C gives the full experimental
details.

Main Results. As shown in Table 1, under the same underlying model, general coding agents perform
similarly to one another in the PA2G setting, with gaps of at most 2.50 points, and GPT-5.6-Luna [35] does
not turn image generation into a visual advantage in the P2G setting. OpenGame, although designed for
game development, does not outperform general coding agents, suggesting that it may not generalize to tasks
beyond its built-in templates or adapt well to the demo-recording requirements of GameCraft-Bench.
In
contrast, with GPT-5.6-Luna, VibeGame leads in all four categories and improves the overall score over the
strongest baseline by 11.70 points, showing that our harness substantially strengthens weaker models. With
the frontier model GPT-6.1-Sol, VibeGame trails Codex (P2G) by less than one point in Core Mechanics
and Functional Visuals but leads it by 4.76 and 7.72 points in Content Depth and Art & Presentation,
outperforming it by 4.19 points overall. This suggests that frontier models can already implement core
mechanics and reasonable visuals on their own, but still fall short in building games with deep content and
polished presentation, which is where VibeGame adds its value. Across game types (Figure 4(a)), VibeGame

We select the qualitative cases from GameCraft-Bench (Figure 5). The left case is Sports Skateboard Park, where the agent needs to implement trick system in which the player chains flip, grind, and grab tricks into combos. VibeGame presents aerial tricks such as board flips in consistent and appealing visual style, while Codex (PA2G) draws the character and environment with programmatic shapes (i.e., simple shapes drawn in code), which gives the game crude art style. VibeGame fulfills this requirement with complete attack animations and mechanics that include wind-up tells. Codex (P2G) also produces polished visuals but does not show the opponents wind-up.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We present VibeGame, framework for end-to-end prompt-to-game development that integrates an AI-native game engine, an adversarial agent team, and training-free self-evolution. Under the same underlying model, VibeGame, without any provided assets, outperforms all evaluated agent harnesses; even with the frontier model GPT-6.1-Sol, it improves over the strongest baseline, Codex (P2G), by 4.19 points.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: While VibeGame delivers strong results across diverse game genres, we recognize that several directions remain open for future work. First, we focus on 2D games and have not yet validated the framework in more complex 3D scenes or used it to develop complete commercial games that sustain long-term play. Second, our AI-native design principles are implemented on web-based 2D engine; bringing them to established engines such as Godot [3], so that agents can also operate existing game projects, is promising extension.

sections.title: A Evaluation Details
sections.content: We port the evaluation protocol of GameCraft-Bench from Godot to Phaser: each harness submits its game together with replayable input traces; an automated pipeline checks that the game builds, then replays and records every trace, and the judge model scores each recording against the rubric; each requirements score is then aggregated over the demos as specified by the rubric. We average the scores of three judge passes to reduce judge variance. GameCraft-Bench scores each game with task-specific rubric whose requirements fall into four categories: Core Mechanics (M ), Content Depth (D), Functional Visuals (V ), and Art & Presentation (A). Each category score is the mean of its requirement scores, and the overall score is Overall = BUILD (wM + wDD + wV + wAA), where BUILD is 0 if the game cannot be built or played and 1 otherwise. The weights (wM , wD, wV , wA) are specified by each tasks rubric in GameCraft-Bench. Table 3 Results on the GameCraft-Bench subset scored by the GPT-5.5 judge (mean of its passes). sections.content: C.1 Setup Every harness, including VibeGame, has 24-hour budget per task and runs its model at the xhigh reasoning effort. In the P2G setting, harnesses without native image generation tool are given GPT-Image-2 [31], the same image generation model used by VibeGame, as an external tool together with its documentation. The judge GPT-6.1-Sol runs with medium reasoning effort, and scoring follows the original benchmark (Appendix A). All results are obtained from our own runs and evaluation rather than reused from GameCraftBench, because we changed the engine and modified the task instructions. For w/ Experience, we let VibeGame with GPT-6.1-Sol build and self-evolve on 5 tasks randomly sampled from outside the ablation set, using the task rubrics and the vision-language model (VLM) judge scores in place of user feedback. We then add the evolved artifacts to the initial project of VibeGame with GPT-5.6Luna and let it build the ablation tasks. C.2 Task Instructions To close the gap between the quality of game and what its demos show, we add the following demo hint to the original instructions: > All scoring is done from these recordings alone your source code is never read. feature no demo shows does not count, however well it is built. Use the full 20 each demo allows rather than cutting off after few seconds, keep each state on screen long enough to read, and show as many distinct assets and element types as each scene plausibly supports. We also use Phaser instead of Godot as the game engine, so we do not claim that our results are comparable with those reported on the original GameCraft-Bench. 18 C.2.1 VibeGame /vibegame-build # Cardgame Autobattler Build Cardgame Autobattler at `/workspace/cardgame-autobattler/`. This is not prototype. It is **complete, shippable micro-game** that could sit on an itch.io page or Steam as polished vertical slice. ## Core Vision draft-and-watch autobattler where the player recruits creatures from shared shop each round, arranges them on board, and watches them fight automatically against an opponent's team. Strategy lives entirely in the draft phase: which creatures to buy, when to level up for stronger units, and how to build synergies between tribal tags. Creatures of the same tribe buff each other stack enough Beasts and they gain attack; fill row with Undead and they resurrect once. An 8-player elimination format (simulated against AI) creates escalating pressure as the field narrows. The fantasy is assembling dream team from random offerings and watching your synergy engine demolish the opposition. ## What the Player Experiences 1. **Title Screen** tavern interior with the game name on wooden sign above the bar, creature silhouettes seated at tables, and "Find Match" button styled as tavern door. No unstyled blank page. 2. **Shop Phase** Each round, shop displays 3-5 random creatures for purchase. The player buys creatures (spending gold), places them on bench or directly onto the board (limited slots). Selling creatures refunds partial gold. timer counts down to the fight phase. 3. **Board Arrangement** The player's board has front row and back row. Positioning matters: front-row creatures are attacked first; back-row creatures with ranged attacks stay safe longer. Drag-and-drop placement. 4. **Auto Combat** When the timer expires, the player's board fights an opponent's board automatically. Creatures attack in order, targeting the nearest enemy. Abilities trigger based on conditions (on-attack, on-death, start-of-combat). The fight plays out with attack animations and health bars depleting. 5. **Tribal Synergies** At least 5 tribes (Beast, Undead, Mech, Dragon, Elemental). Having 2/4/6 of tribe activates escalating bonuses shown in synergy tracker panel. Synergies are the primary strategic axis. 6. **Economy** Gold income increases each round. Winning streaks and losing streaks both grant bonus gold. Interest accrues on saved gold (1 gold per 10 saved). Levelling up costs gold but increases shop quality and board size. 7. **Elimination** The player starts with health pool. Losing round costs health proportional to surviving enemy creatures. Last player standing wins. placement screen shows final ranking. ## Project layout ``` /workspace/cardgame-autobattler/ project.json index.html demo_outputs/ scripts/ scenes/ engine and scene entry points the game loads here <- your input traces (1-10 files) assets/ config/ ``` The evaluator loads `index.html` in headless browser at 1280x720. The game must reach playable state with no fatal console errors: that launch is gate, and project failing it scores zero no matter what the demos show. ## Running it yourself The container has no display, so browser can only run headless. `vibegame run` defaults to visible browser and will fail without one: ``` vibegame run . -b --headless vibegame play status ``` ## Demos # serve the game and take runtime control # inspect the running scene Ship **110 input-trace files** under `demo_outputs/`, one per demo, each named `*.json`. The evaluator launches fresh game per trace, replays your trace as synthetic mouse and keyboard input at 1280720, and records the screen. Only the first 10 traces by filename are evaluated; recordings longer than 20 are sampled from random 20 window. > All scoring is done from these recordings alone your source code is never read. feature no demo shows does not count, however well it is built. Use the full 20 each demo allows rather than cutting off after few seconds, keep each state on screen long enough to read, and show as many distinct assets and element types as each scene plausibly supports. ### Scenarios Normal play should start from the title screen and demonstrate the task's core gameplay loop. Demo playback must be deterministic. For demos that need specific state (a specific level, combat state, upgrade screen, result state, or late-game setup), define named scenarios your game loads when launched with: ``` 19 index.html?scenario=<id> ``` When `scenario=<id>` is present the game must skip menus, set up the named state deterministically (seed any RNG), and begin accepting input immediately. ### Trace file format ```json { "scenario": "title_flow", "duration_frames": 360, "events": [ "type": "mouse_click", "button": "left", "x": 300, "y": 360}, {"frame": 30, "keycode": "1"}, {"frame": 90, "type": "key_press", {"frame": 180, "type": "key_press", "keycode": "SPACE"}, {"frame": 300, "type": "wait"} ] } ``` - `scenario` optional; omit for normal game launch from the title screen. - `duration_frames` total frames to record at 30 fps; cap at **600 (20 s)**. - `events` time-ordered inputs. Coordinates are pixels in the 1280720 viewport. Supported types: - `mouse_click`: `{frame, type, button: "left""right", x, y}` - `mouse_down` / `mouse_up`: `{frame, type, button: "left""right", x, y}` use these for drag interactions: emit `mouse_down` at the start point, one or more `mouse_move` events along the way, and `mouse_up` at the end. `mouse_click` is `mouse_down` + `mouse_up` at the same point in tight succession. - `mouse_move`: `{frame, type, x, y}` - `key_press` / `key_down` / `key_up`: `{frame, type, keycode}` keycodes: `A``Z`, `0``9`, `ESCAPE`, `ENTER`, `SPACE`, `TAB`, `BACKSPACE`, `DELETE`, `SHIFT`, `CTRL`, `ALT`, `UP`, `DOWN`, `LEFT`, `RIGHT`. - `wait`: `{frame, type}` anchor frame, no input. Replay must be deterministic: same trace, fresh launch, same outcome every time. The first line of the instruction invokes the one-shot mode of VibeGame through the vibegame-build skill, whose prompt is as follows: --- name: vibegame-build description: Run VibeGame's standard end-to-end game development workflow with reviewer gates. Use when the user wants to create game from zero or evolve an existing game across multiple stages. --- # VibeGame Build This is **long-running delegation workflow**. The lead sets multi-stage implementation plan (potentially hours of work), delegates to teammates, and supervises execution. The lead **does not implement directly** only tiny local edits qualify as self-service. Core lead responsibilities in this mode: - **Understand**: rebuild context from code, specs, and live verification - **Architect**: design the multi-stage plan before any execution - **Supervise**: delegate, track progress, and course-correct through teammates --- ## Phase 1: Plan Clarify the goal until it is concrete and actionable. Do not proceed to execution until the goal is aligned. This goal is not native CLI goal, such as one set with `create_goal`. native goal starts new turn each time you stop. That works against this workflow: you stop while teammates work, and their reports wake you. `.vibegame/goal.md` `## User Input` holds the user's verbatim request, written there by hook when this build was invoked. Confirm it is non-empty before anything else; if empty, paste the user's original words in yourself, unedited. GDD, `prd.md` and the final review all answer to it. 1. Use at most 3 Task-tool subagents (Claude Code `Explore` / Codex equivalent NOT teammates spawned via `vibegame lead`) to inspect three discovery surfaces in parallel: - **Current codebase** existing files, patterns, specs, implementation status. - **`modules/index.md`** catalog of installed `*Module.js` Node scripts (one-line description + interface per module). Anything you can wire in directly via `script: "XxxModule"` or extend by subclassing is work the team does not have to redo. - **`skeletons/index.md`** catalog of available sub-genre skeletons. For any slug whose row matches the request, open `skeletons/<slug>/index.md` and summarize what `scripts/`, `entities/`, and `scenes/` could be cherry-picked into the new 20 project. Treat the skeleton as head start, not constraint. 2. If gameplay mechanics are involved (movement, combat, enemies, bosses, HUD, hit feedback, death, pacing basically anything beyond static viewer), **commission `designer` to fill the design-layer gaps before decomposing tasks** and update `GDD.md` for user to review. - Whenever GDD changes designer's handoff or your own edit check it against the verbatim request before moving on: ```sh cat .vibegame/goal.md .vibegame/GDD.md > /tmp/gdd-fidelity.md vibegame vlm -t /tmp/gdd-fidelity.md -s "You compare game design document against the user's verbatim request. List every requirement the GDD omits, weakens, or contradicts. Quote both sides. If none, reply exactly: NO DEVIATION." ``` - Anything but `NO DEVIATION` goes back to `designer` with the quoted lines. This check is mandatory; your own read of the GDD does not replace it you wrote the brief it was derived from. 3. If visual elements are involved: - If user does not provide concept/reference image, commission `artist` to produce **project reference image** (see artist.md "Reference image"): restrained single image showing the **actual in-game look** from the GDD (not concept art / mood board / poster), containing only the key elements that belong in the same real gameplay view. Later asset tasks use this image as the reference so generated player, enemy, UI, prop, and scene assets match the approved elements. - Establish the GDD before commissioning the reference image. Artist may develop visual details and UI layouts left unspecified by the GDD, but must preserve its established gameplay rules and requirements. - If the generated reference image contradicts or extends the GDD, the lead must reconcile them before execution: either ask `artist` to redraw the reference to match the GDD, or update the GDD to explicitly accept UI / HUD / layout / prop choices introduced by the reference image. - Use this reference image to validate visual direction with the user. Iterate until approved. - DO NOT specify frame counts or animation details - that is artist's responsibility 4. Break the goal into macro stages. Each stage should have: - The project state reached when the stage completes - How that stage outcome can be tested - Which earlier stages must finish first - Tasks that can launch together once the stage is ready 5. **Within each stage, choose independent tasks that can run in parallel.** For each task: - Single bounded deliverable with clear ownership - Clear acceptance criteria - No hidden dependency on another task in the same stage - If proposed sibling tasks share an unstable core interface, state model, scene structure, or core files, merge them into one task 6. Fill in `.vibegame/goal.md`: `## Task Breakdown` (stage plan and tasks) and `## Done When` (goal-specific, checkable outcomes not "the game runs"). Never edit `## User Input`; when the user overrides an earlier requirement, express it in `## Done When`. 7. **Give the files for user to review. Wait for explicit user approval before execution.** The user may direct you to merge / split / drop tasks at this stage accept their direction. Task scope is the user's decision, not yours. Examples: - Coherent first playable plus parallel art: - Stage 0: `vertical-slice` builds the playable loop; `art-pack` produces final runtime assets. - Stage 1: `visual-integration` swaps assets in, tunes composition, and removes temporary visuals. - Stage 2: `final-review` verifies the complete goal. - Interface-first parallel systems: - Stage 0: Orchestrator writes stable scene, event, collision, and data interfaces into the task specs; `player`, `boss`, and `map` implement fully parallel systems against those interfaces; each task includes standalone test scene. - Stage 1: `system-integration` connects the systems and resolves cross-system feel. - Stage 2: `asset-replacement` swaps placeholder visuals for final assets. > DO NOT spawn reviewer in this stage, otherwise you cannot stop and request for user approval. --- ## Phase 2: Run Delegate to teammates and supervise through to completion. 1. Spawn reviewer agent as **persistent team member** in the VibeGame build workflow. This reviewer stays alive for the entire session -- do NOT spawn new reviewer per stage or per request. All review requests go to this same instance. Tell it: "You are in the VibeGame build workflow, the user's goal is ..." and reviewer need to do: 1. Create `.vibegame/review-lock.json` with `{"locked": true}`, and never release it before final goal is achieved 2. Learn about the detailed goal and plan from `.vibegame/goal.md`, `.vibegame/GDD.md`, and relevant specs to understand the goal before any review begins. 3. Learn about the current codebase and wait for the final review request. 2. For each stage: - Create and initialize all tasks with `vibegame lead task create / init` - **Spawn parallel programmer agents for independent tasks** -- do NOT wait for one to finish before starting the next if they have no dependencies. Use `--blocked-by` to declare dependencies. - Follow `.vibegame/orchestrator.md` for the full task pipeline (architect programmer auditor player) - After the stage is complete, update the progress checklist in `.vibegame/goal.md` 3. After all stages are complete, notify the reviewer that all tasks are done and request final review. Use the review request message format in `src/.vibegame/orchestrator.md` `## Use reviewer for final quality gate`. 4. Read reviewer's reports via `vibegame lead read --name reviewer` and arrange fixes as findings arrive while reviewer continues testing, following `.vibegame/orchestrator.md`. The reviewer will release the lock after approving the final goal. If 21 it ends with reject verdict, address outstanding feedback and request review again (same message format, updated evidence). Remember the reviewer always has to review all final quality gates instead of just checking new fixes. --- ## Rules - **Never implement directly** unless the change is trivial few-line edit. - Lead owns understanding, architecture, and supervision not code. - **Reviewer is persistent**: spawn it ONCE at session start, send all review requests to the same instance. Never spawn second reviewer. - Reviewer does **not** do per-stage reviews. It only reviews once at the end after all tasks are done. - review-lock.json is owned by the reviewer agent, not the lead. - Keep stages macro-level. Detailed implementation belongs to architect and programmer agents. - **Maximize parallelism**: spawn independent programmer agents simultaneously. Waiting sequentially for tasks that could run in parallel wastes the team's capacity. - Use `vibegame lead task create --blocked-by` to declare dependencies. Tasks without blockers should start immediately. - Follow `.vibegame/orchestrator.md` once execution begins. ## Useful Commands ```sh vibegame lead task create "<description>" --name <name> vibegame lead task init "<name>" --use-worktree ``` ## review-lock.json This file is created by the reviewer on spawn and is released only after the final goal is approved. It is not stage-gate mechanism. C.2.2 Baselines, PA2G # Cardgame Autobattler Build Cardgame Autobattler at `/workspace/cardgame-autobattler/`. This is not prototype. Strategy lives entirely in the draft phase: which creatures to buy, when to level up for stronger units, and how to build synergies between tribal tags. sections.title: D Demonstrations
sections.content: We demonstrate VibeGame in two scenarios: creating game from new request (Game Creation), which corresponds to the P2G task defined in Section 1, and continuing to edit an existing project (Game Edit). Unless otherwise noted, the demonstrations use the automatic-by-default setting described in Section 3.2.3: after the user approves the request, the orchestrator continues development until reviewer acceptance, while the user may still interrupt the process with feedback. The prompt boxes in the figures report the final user-approved request rather than interface commands or intermediate clarification turns. Figure 9 Game creation demonstrations. Top: Pixel Sekiro, pixel-art boss fight created from text prompt. Bottom: Hollow Knight boss slice, side-scrolling boss fight created from gameplay prompt and concept image. 27 Figure 10 Game edit demonstrations. Top: intellectual property (IP) transfer, replacing the visual theme while preserving gameplay logic. Middle: genre transfer, converting turn-based card game into real-time boss fight while preserving its visual identity. Bottom: rule transfer, swapping the player and boss roles while preserving their abilities and animations. D.1 Game Creation Game creation starts from text request and optional reference images and exercises the full loop from intention alignment to project delivery. In this paper, we report results for both text-only and multimodal requests. D.1.1 Text Input To test creation driven by compact text request, we asked the system to build Sekiro-style 2D boss fight: retro pixel-art duel recreating the reed-field battle between Sekiro and Genichiro. The request specified the combat rules in few sentences: the player can defend, perform frame-perfect deflections, attack, step-dodge, jump, slash in the air, and execute deathblow once the boss posture is broken; the boss can defend and deflect, and special attacks are made readable through delayed wind-up frames. The system started from an existing side-scrolling action skeleton, inheriting its scene structure and UI modules. However, Sekiros core is deflection-posture system entirely different from the skeletons simple hitpoint-based combat, requiring the system to build the combat layer from scratch: both sides have independent posture gauges, defense distinguishes regular blocking from frame-perfect deflection, boss attacks are divided into blockable normal attacks and perilous attacks requiring specific responses, and full posture gauge triggers multi-stage deathblow animation. The final output comprised 12 scripts, 2 character asset packs, 11 visual effect entities, and 1 UI asset pack. This case demonstrates how short request that names genre convention is expanded into complete, correctly tuned combat system. The first row of Figure 9 shows the request and resulting combat sequence. D.1.2 Multimodal Input To test multimodal creation, we provided text request together with an author-created concept image for Hollow Knight-style 1v1 boss fight. The text request specified the mechanical scope: the player has basic attack, charged attack, dash, jump, and an aerial attack, while the boss combines two melee skills with ranged attack on side-scrolling arena 1.5x the camera width. The concept image anchored the character designs, the ruined-cathedral arena, and the overall visual atmosphere, which the generated assets were required to match. The second row of Figure 9 showcases the multimodal input and resulting game. We can observe that the delivered slice realizes both sides of this specification. The boss gates its melee sweep, ground slam, and 28 arcing projectile on the players distance, keeps its preferred range, and can be staggered out of idle; the players five actions cover the full movement-attack loop, including dash invincibility frames and aerial slashes; hit feedback combines screen shake, flash, and spark particles, with mask-style health icons and full-width boss bar completing the heads-up display (HUD). All character and arena art was generated to match the concept image, preserving its silhouette language and cold palette. This case demonstrates how text can specify gameplay rules while the concept image anchors visual identity. D.2 Game Edit The next cases begin from accepted projects and alter different layers of the existing game. Specifically, in this paper, we report three types of editing: (1) intellectual property (IP) transfer that changes visual assets while preserving mechanics; (2) genre transfer that replaces the central gameplay while preserving visual identity; and (3) rule transfer that changes the roles of existing characters while reusing their abilities and animations. D.2.

sections.title: IP Transfer
sections.content: Starting from completed side-scrolling boss fight project, we ask the system to replace the entire games visual theme with Kung Fu Panda IP. The system regenerates all art assets (including characters, effects, UI, and background), and then adjusts configurations for the new sprite size and frame counts. The delivered project retains the original combat logic, illustrating an edit concentrated on the asset and configuration layers. See top row of Figure 10. This validates the code-asset decoupling in the engine: when the project structure is well designed, IP transfer is accomplished primarily through asset replacement, with no need to rewrite core logic. D.2.2 Genre Transfer Starting from completed turn-based card game project, we ask the system to change the core gameplay from card strategy to real-time action boss fight. This is deep transformation: the turn-based card-playing mechanic was completely replaced with real-time melee, dodging, and shooting, while the system preserved the original projects cyberpunk visual style and character designs. Unlike IP transfer where only assets change, genre transfer requires the system to judge what can be preserved and what must be rewritten, demonstrating the systems ability to perform selective deep modification while maintaining overall consistency (Figure 10, middle row). D.2.3 Rule Transfer Starting from the Hollow Knight-style boss fight created from multimodal input in Section D.1.2, we tested the systems ability to handle unconventional creative requests by asking it to swap the player and boss roles, requiring only that each character keep its existing abilities and animations. In that source game, the player controlled small horned warrior, while the antlered boss moved autonomously with melee slam, lunge, and ranged thorn volley. The edit enlarges the former player character into an AI-driven boss and shrinks the former boss into the player-controlled character, so the player now wields the former bosss moveset while the former player character fights autonomously with its own dash, charged slash, and aerial attack. This request is not simple asset exchange: the system must convert the former boss AI into player control scheme, turn the former players manual controls into autonomous boss AI, rebind inputs, and remap the HUD and win/lose flow, all without adding any new art or moves. Our system completed this transformation (Figure 10, bottom row), demonstrating that it can restructure gameplay roles in response to non-standard edit requests.

sections.title: E More Demonstrations
sections.content: Beyond the cases analyzed in Appendix D, we used VibeGame to build broader range of games spanning multiple genres and input modalities. Each game was produced from natural language prompt, some accompanied by reference image, exercising the same pipeline described in the main text. Together they 29 illustrate the breadth of game types the system handles, from real-time action and arcade games to turn-based strategy and an LLM-driven social-deduction game.

sections.content: A fruit-slicing arcade game built from text-only request (Figure 11). Each fruit splits into two physically simulated halves with fruit-specific weight, bounce, and juice effects; the game includes pointer-driven slicing, combo scoring, missed-fruit indicators, and game-over state. Figure 11 three-fruit combo sliced mid-air with split halves and juice effects.

sections.content: Three defects from one run of VibeGame with GPT-6.1-Sol on the GameCraft-Bench task Open-World Beast Tamer [11], each reported by different review role. Quotes are the agents own reports. Auditor (static review). The PRD asks the player to tap when the timing indicator is inside its acceptance band (beats at 1, 2, 4, and 5 s, 0.3 s). Figure 18 shows the game before and after the repair. AdventureUI.js:5354 renders four equally spaced flex cards and an indicator at elapsed / 6 . . . Beat centers 1/2/4/5 and 0.3/0.45 exist only as text; no band-position/width . . . is computed from the scoring predicates. . . . This is missing timing-to-presentation mapping, not visual-quality judgment. 36 Figure 18 Auditor case, before (top) and after (bottom). After the repair, each band is placed and sized by its tapping window on one time axis. Placeholder art; the bottom image shows the physics debug overlay. Player (runtime check). An independent VLM pass first flagged the completed map; the player confirmed it and measured it in the running game. Figure 19 shows the game before and after the repair. completed-map owned opportunity buttons visibly truncate names and type/status qualifiers with ellipses. Examples: Heartcamp Frost Gate P. . . label-overflow.json shows actual scroll widths exceeding client widths. . . . 37 Figure 19 Player case, before (top) and after (bottom). After the repair, every entry shows its full name, type, and status. Reviewer (final check). Found by stopping the game 120 frames after an ability and reading both characters positions. Figure 20 shows the game before and after the repair. after normal successful Fire Breath, waiting idle for two seconds leaves Emberlynx and the standing keeper at the exact same ground anchor, producing an inseparable/occluded central silhouette. VLM . . . FAIL: the orange body reads as flames attached to the keeper, not companion. 38 Figure 20 Reviewer case, before (top) and after (bottom). After the repair, the companion stands beside the keeper. Codex with the AI-Native Engine To isolate the effect of the AI-native engine, we equip the native Codex harness with the engine of VibeGame. Both settings use GPT-6.1-Sol on all 30 tasks in the PA2G setting with the same asset library. With the engine, the overall score of Codex rises from 64.44 to 67.13, with gains in all four categories  (Table 5)  . Since the art in both settings comes from the same asset library, we attribute the improvement to the engine; the 39 largest gain, in Content Depth, suggests that the structured project representation helps agents expand game content. Table 5 Codex with and without the AI-native engine of VibeGame (GPT-6.1-Sol, PA2G, all 30 tasks). Columns as in Table 1. Harness Codex w/ Engine 80.21 82.41 58.42 62.37 57.51 58.94 66.52 68. Overall 64.44 67.13 Limitation of Self-Evolution We observe that when VibeGame continuously develops games of different types, the experience accumulated by self-evolution can instead lower agent performance. Future work should analyze this phenomenon further and separate general experience from genre-specific experience, so that each can be injected adaptively. This observation is also one of the motivations for our experimental design: the main experiments use VibeGame without any accumulated experience, and we evaluate self-evolution separately in the ablation study.
